'''''Washingtonia filifera''''', commonly known as the '''California fan palm''', '''cotton palm''' or '''desert fan palm''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=Washingtonia filifera (California Fan Palm) |url=https://toptropicals.com/catalog/uid/washingtonia_filifera.htm?srsltid=AfmBOorl5sKXydajTCDTz8-wKGo2dLdNQnRRdyC-iQU20mK_3ckEet1D |website=Top Tropicals}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cornett |first1=J. W. |date=1986 |title=The Common Name of Washingtonia filifera |journal=Principes |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=153–55}}</ref> is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Arecaceae]], native to the far [[southwestern United States]] and northwestern [[Mexico]]. It typically grows {{convert|30-50|ft|m|0}} tall and {{convert|1-2|ft|m|1}} wide,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Washingtonia filifera |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/tree/wasfil/all.html |access-date=2025-09-28 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref> with a sturdy, columnar trunk and waxy, fan-shaped ([[palmate]]) leaves. As a [[Monocotyledon|monocot]], it is evergreen and exhibits a tree-like growth habit.

It is the only palm species native to the [[southwestern United States]], forming groves around [[Perennial water|perennial water sources]] in the [[Colorado Desert|Colorado]], [[Mojave Desert|Mojave]], and [[Sonoran Desert|Sonoran deserts]].<ref name=":1" /> These stands provide critical habitat for wildlife and were historically used by [[Indigenous peoples of California|Indigenous peoples]] of the region for food, shelter, and materials.<ref name=":2" /> Today the California fan palm is widely planted as an ornamental tree in arid and subtropical climates, though wild populations face pressures from groundwater decline, and habitat alteration.

In California, where the majority of its native groves occur, the species forms iconic desert oases such as the Oasis of Mara in [[Joshua Tree National Park]], the Thousand Palms Oasis in the [[Coachella Valley Preserve]], [[Lost Palms Oasis Trail|Lost Palms Oasis]], and [[Fortynine Palms Oasis]]. Outside California, notable populations are protected at Castle Creek<ref name=":0" /> in Arizona's [[Bradshaw Mountains]], the [[Hassayampa River Preserve]], and [[Kofa National Wildlife Refuge]].

==Description==
''Washingtonia filifera'' var. ''filifera'' is a stout, single-stemmed palm that typically grows {{convert|30-50|ft|m|0}} tall.<ref name=":3" /> The trunk is usually {{convert|1-2|ft|m|1}} thick,<ref name=":3" /> brown when exposed but often concealed beneath a dense skirt of persistent dead fronds. If left untrimmed, this thatch may extend the full length of the trunk, providing insulation against both heat and cold, reducing fire damage, and creating shelter for small animals.<ref name=":3" />
[[File:Washingtonia filifera and Carnegiea gigantea at Alkali Spring, Castle Creek, Arizona.jpg|thumb|California fan palms (''Washingtonia filifera'') with dense thatch skirts, growing alongside saguaros ''([[Saguaro|Carnegiea gigantea]]'') at Alkali Spring in the Castle Creek area, [[Yavapai County, Arizona|Yavapai County]], Arizona. This grove is located on private land owned by [[Castle Hot Springs (Arizona)|Castle Hot Springs Resort]].]]
The [[Crown (botany)|crown]] consists of large, fan-shaped ([[Glossary of leaf morphology|palmate]]) leaves borne on petioles. Petiole edges carry relatively small, blunt teeth compared with the more heavily armed [[Washingtonia filifera var. robusta|Mexican fan palm]]<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Comment peut-on voir la différence entre le Washingtonia filifera et le robusta? {{!}} La Palmeraie fr |url=http://palmvrienden.net/frlapalmeraie/2016/05/comment-peut-on-voir-la-difference-entre-le-washingtonia-filifera-et-le-robusta/ |access-date=2025-09-28 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> [[Washingtonia filifera var. robusta|(''W. f. var. robusta'')]], and their bases are predominantly green rather than reddish or brown.<ref name=":5" /> The fronds themselves are a distinctive gray-blue-green, a color often used as a marker of genetic purity in the species.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Villanueva-Almanza|first1=Lorena|last2=Landis|first2=Jacob B.|last3=Koenig|first3=Daniel|last4=Ezcurra|first4=E.|date=March 2021|title=Genetic and morphological differentiation in Washingtonia (Arecaceae): solving a century-old palm mystery|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/350004102|journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society|volume=196|issue=4|pages=506–523|doi=10.1093/botlinnean/boab009}}</ref> Between the [[Leaflet (botany)|leaf segments]] are long, threadlike white fibers; in young individuals especially, these filaments can resemble tufts of cotton, giving rise to the informal name "cotton palm."

The [[Inflorescence]]s are long, branched [[Spadix (botany)|spadices]] that extend beyond the [[frond]]s and carry small, cream-colored flowers in late summer.<ref name=":3" /> The fruit is a black [[drupe]] about 1–2 cm (0.4–0.8 in) in diameter, [[ripening]] in autumn and containing a single seed. Mature palms can produce thousands of fruits in a season, which are dispersed mainly by [[coyote]]s, [[fox]]es, and [[bird]]s. Coyote dispersal is especially effective, with seeds carried long distances and showing improved [[germination]] after digestion.<ref name=":3" />

California fan palms typically live 80–150 years, with some individuals estimated to reach about 200 years.<ref name=":3" /> They are well adapted to arid desert climates, surviving with minimal supplemental water and drawing heavily on groundwater through deep or shallow root systems depending on local conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Find Trees & Learn {{!}} UA Campus Arboretum |url=https://apps.cals.arizona.edu/arboretum |access-date=2025-09-28 |website=apps.cals.arizona.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3" />

Documented ambient extremes within its native range include summer highs up to about '''57 °C (134 °F)''', such as at [[Furnace Creek, California|Furnace Creek]],<ref name=":6" /> and winter lows near '''-11 °C (12–13 °F)'''.<ref name=":3" />

==Taxonomy==
The [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''filifera'' means 'thread-bearing' in Latin.<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=UK| isbn=978-1-84533-731-5 }}</ref>

[[Plants of the World Online]] (POWO) currently recognizes three distinct infraspecifics of ''Washingtonia filifera'': <ref name="POWO">{{cite taxon|POWO|id=267788-2|title=''Washingtonia filifera'' (T.Moore & Mast.) H.Wendl. ex de Bary|access-date=February 4, 2026}}</ref>

* ''Washingtonia filifera'' var. ''filifera''

* [[Washingtonia filifera var. robusta|''Washingtonia filifera'' var.'' robusta'' (H.Wendl.) Parish]]

* ''Washingtonia filifera'' var. ''sonorae'' (S.Watson) M.E.Jones

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Washingtonia filifera'' var. ''filifera'' is the only palm species native to the [[southwestern United States]], and the vast majority of its populations occur in [[southern California]]. Here it dominates spring-fed and stream-fed oases across the [[Colorado Desert]],<ref name=":1">{{cite book |last=Cornett |first=James W. |title=The Sonoran Desert: A Brief Natural History |date=1997 |publisher=Palm Springs Desert Museum |isbn=0-937794-27-9 |location=Palm Springs, California}}</ref> with additional scattered stands in the [[Mojave Desert]].<ref name=":6">{{cite book |last=Cornett |first=James W. |title=Naturalized Populations of the Desert Fan Palm, Washingtonia filifera, in Death Valley National Monument in Plant Biology of Eastern California |date=1987 |publisher=White Mountain Research Station, University of California |location=Los Angeles |pages=167–74}}</ref>

=== Arizona ===
Outside California, the largest U.S. population is in central Arizona's lower [[Bradshaw Mountains]],<ref name=":0" /> where several groves occur along Castle Creek, a tributary of the [[Agua Fria River]]. Some of these groves lie on [[Bureau of Land Management]] land, while others are on private property. Along Castle Creek, the main spring sites are Dripping and Alkali Spring. 
[[File:Washingtonia filifera grove at Dripping Spring, Castle Creek, Arizona.jpg|center|thumb|500x500px|A grove of California fan palms (''Washingtonia filifera'' var. ''filifera'') at Dripping Spring in the Castle Creek area, [[Yavapai County, Arizona|Yavapai County]], [[Arizona]]. The site is managed by the [[Bureau of Land Management|U.S. Bureau of Land Management (BLM)]].]]Castle Creek has also been proposed as the possible source of the seed from which ''Washingtonia filifera'' was first formally described in 1879, based on 19th-century reports and geographic coordinates that align closely with the site.<ref name=":0" /> Other Arizona populations are found along the [[Gila River]] near [[Yuma, Arizona|Yuma]],<ref>{{Cite web |author=Nothaft, Mark |date=22 March 2016 |title=Are palm trees native to Arizona? |url=http://www.azcentral.com/story/news/local/phoenix-contributor/2016/03/22/palm-trees-native-arizona/82106610/ |access-date=26 March 2016 |quote=Mark Fleming, curator of botany at the Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum of Tucson, says ''Washingtonia filifera'', or the California fan palm, is the state's only naturally occurring variety and that they are found in pockets around southern California, Northern Mexico, and one or two pockets in Arizona.}}</ref> at the [[Hassayampa River Preserve]] and nearby [https://www.dflt.org/projects-1-2/new-river-nature-reserve New River Preserve] in [[Maricopa County, Arizona|Maricopa County]], in portions of [[Pima County, Arizona|Pima]] and [[Pinal County, Arizona|Pinal]] counties, and along the [[Colorado River]] in [[Mohave County, Arizona|Mohave County]]. Although the species is considered globally secure, it is classified as critically imperiled ([[NatureServe conservation status|S1]]) within Arizona due to its limited and fragmented distribution.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Maricopa County Parks & Recreation |date=September 29, 2025 |title=Natural Resource Master Plan |url=https://www.maricopacountyparks.net/assets/1/6/NATURAL_RESOURCE_PLAN_2024.pdf}}</ref>

=== Nevada ===

In Nevada, isolated groves occur in [[Clark County, Nevada|Clark County]], specifically at the [[Warm Springs Natural Area]], [https://juanitaspringsranch.com/ Juanita Springs Ranch], [https://www.nps.gov/lake/learn/nature/rogers-spring.htm Rogers Spring], and [https://www.tophotsprings.com/blue-point-spring-nevada/ Blue Point Spring].<ref name="Spencer_Foreword" /><ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Cornett |first=James W. |date=1988 |title=The Occurrence of the Desert Fan Palm, Washingtonia filifera, in Southern Nevada |url=https://arizona.aws.openrepository.com/handle/10150/609098 |journal=Desert Plants}}</ref>

However, the origin of these populations is debated. Some palms, such as those at Blue Point Spring, are thought to have been planted in the mid-20th century, while others, such as those at Juanita Springs, have been present since at least 1950 and show evidence of longer establishment.<ref name=":8" />[[File:Washingtonia filifera Warm Springs, Nevada.jpg|thumb|250x250px|A grove of California fan palms (''Washingtonia filifera'') in the [[Warm Springs Natural Area]], [[Clark County, Nevada|Clark County]], [[Nevada]].]]

=== Baja California ===
In Mexico, the species is native only to Baja California, extending south to [[Bahía de los Ángeles]].<ref name=":7">{{cite book |last1=Wiggins |first1=Ira L. |title=Flora of Baja California |date=1980 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=0-8047-1016-3 |location=Stanford, California |page=1025}}</ref>

It has also become naturalized in warm springs near [[Death Valley]], in extreme northwest Sonora, and in scattered locations in [[Texas]], [[Florida]], [[Hawaii]], [[Utah]], the [[United States Virgin Islands|U.S. Virgin Island]], and overseas in [[Australia]], [[Morocco]], [[Egypt]], [[Iraq]], [[Spain]], and [[Italy]].<ref name="WCSP">{{cite web |author=Govaerts, R. |title=Washingtonia filifera (Rafarin) H.Wendl. ex de Bary, Bot. Zeitung (Berlin) 37: LXI (1879). |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=214250 |access-date=21 June 2014 |work=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families}}</ref><ref name="USDA">{{cite web |title=Plant Profile for Washingtonia filifera (California fan palm) |url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=WAFI |access-date=20 June 2014 |work=Natural Resources Conservation Service |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Washingtonia filifera grove (Palm Springs).jpg|thumb|A grove of ''Washingtonia filifera'' south of Palm Springs.]]
California fan palms provide habitat for the [[Dinapate wrightii|giant palm-boring beetle]], [[western yellow bat]], [[hooded oriole]], and many other bird species. Hooded orioles rely on the trees for food and places to build nests. Numerous insect species visit the hanging inflorescences that appear in late spring.<ref>Cornett, J. W. 1986. Arthropod visitors at Washingtonia filifera (Wendl) Flowers. Pan Pacific Entomologist 62(3):224–25.</ref>

Historically, natural oases are mainly restricted to areas downstream from the source of hot springs, though water is not always visible at the surface.

Today's oasis environment may have been protected from colder climatic changes over the course of its evolution. Thus, this palm is restricted by both water and climate to widely separated [[Relict (biology)|relict]] groves.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.xeri.com/Moapa/relict.htm|title=Desert Fan Palms-Evidence suggests "Relict Genus"|website=www.xeri.com|access-date=2016-12-10}}</ref> The trees in these groves show little if any genetic differentiation (through electrophoretic examination), suggesting that the genus is genetically very stable.

===Fire adaptations===
Fan palm oases have historically been subject to both natural and manmade fires. Fires are rarely fatal for the fan palm, but it is also not completely immune to them.

The fan palm's trunk is heavily resistant to burning. In most cases, the trunk is only at risk of losing some of its outer vascular layers during a fire. After those layers are ignited and burnt off, the remaining surface is left heavily charred, which fortifies the trunk against future flames. Subsequent burnings serve to char the trunk more, further increasing its fire resistance.

The palm's fronds are the most flammable portion of the tree. The unchecked buildup of dead fronds as a 'skirt' around the trunk can be especially dangerous in a crown fire. A severe accumulation of them could constitute enough kindling to completely burn through the trunk, killing the plant. However, if a palm can survive the burning of its fronds, they will take time to regrow, leaving it less susceptible to fire in the meantime.

Barring extreme, fatal conditions, fires are even conducive to the health and propagation of fan palms. The palms' reproduction process benefits from burnings, as fires help release saplings and clear away overgrowth from surrounding vegetation. Fires can also help palms conserve water by burning away their crowns and parts of their trunks, leading to a reduction in surface area and therefore decreased rates of evaporation and transpiration.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vogl, Richard; McHargue, Lawrence|date=1966|title=Vegetation of California Fan Palm Oases on the San Andreas Fault|url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.2307/1933929|journal=Ecological Society of America|volume=47|issue=4|pages=532–40|doi=10.2307/1933929|jstor=1933929|bibcode=1966Ecol...47..532V |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Threats===
Grazing animals can kill young plants through trampling, or by eating the terminus at the apical meristem, the growing portion of the plant. This may have kept palms restricted to a lesser range than indicated by the availability of water.

The palm boring beetle ''[[Dinapate wrightii]]'' ([[Bostrichidae]]) can chew through the trunks of this and other palms. Eventually, a continued infestation of beetles can kill various genera and species of palms. ''W. filifera'' appears to be resistant to the red palm weevil (''[[Rhynchophorus ferrugineus]]'') by a mechanism of [[antibiosis]] – production of compounds lethal to the larvae.<ref name="CISR">{{cite web | url=http://cisr.ucr.edu/red_palm_weevil.html | title=Red Palm Weevil | publisher=[[University of California Riverside]] | work=Center for Invasive Species Research | access-date=20 June 2014 | last1=Nisson | last2=Hodel | last3=Hoddle | first1=N. | first2=D. | first3=M.}}</ref><ref name="Dembilio2009">{{cite journal | title=Are the palms ''Washingtonia filifera'' and ''Chamaerops humilis'' suitable hosts for the red palm weevil, ''Rhynchophorus ferrugineus'' (Col. Curculionidae)? | journal=Journal of Applied Entomology |date=August 2009  | volume=133 | issue=7 | pages=565–67 | doi=10.1111/j.1439-0418.2009.01385.x | last1=Dembilio | last2=Jacas | last3=Llácer | first1=Ó. | first2=J.A. | first3=E.| s2cid=85677945 | hdl=20.500.11939/5124 | hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Monroy|first1=F.|last2=Curir|first2=P.|last3=Clematis|first3=F.|last4=Cangelosi|first4=B.|date=June 2016|title=Susceptibility and possible resistance mechanisms in the palm species Phoenix dactylifera, Chamaerops humilis and Washingtonia filifera against Rhynchophorus ferrugineus (Olivier, 1790) (Coleoptera: Curculionidae)|journal=Bulletin of Entomological Research|language=en|volume=106|issue=3|pages=341–46|doi=10.1017/S000748531500108X|pmid=26976073|s2cid=206225113|issn=0007-4853}}</ref>

Currently, the California fan palm is experiencing a population and range expansion, perhaps due to global warming<ref>{{cite book|last=Cornett|first=James W.|title=Desert Palm Oasis|date=2010|publisher=Nature Trails Press|location=Palm Springs, California|isbn=978-0-937794-42-5|edition=Second}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.xeri.com/Moapa/globalwarm.htm|title=global warming & W. filifera Palms – a rebuttal|website=www.xeri.com|access-date=2016-12-10}}</ref> or [[mustang (horse)|mustang control]].{{citation needed|date=February 2025}}

==Uses==
The sweet fruit pulp of the fan palm is edible.<ref>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-date=1980 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50761-4 |edition=Chanticleer Press|page=325}}</ref> The fruit is eaten raw, cooked, or ground into flour for cakes by Native Americans.<ref name=":2">{{cite book|last=Cornett|first=James W.|title=Indian Uses of Desert Plants|date=2011|publisher=Nature Trails Press|location=Palm Springs, California|isbn=978-0-937794-45-6|edition=Third}}</ref> The [[Cahuilla]] and related tribes use the leaves to make sandals, roof [[thatch]], and baskets. The woody petioles are used to make cooking utensils. The [[Moapa Band of Paiute Indians|Moapa band of Paiutes]] and other [[Southern Paiute people]] have written memories of using this palm's seed, fruit, or leaves for various purposes, including as [[famine food]].<ref name="Spencer_Foreword">{{cite web | url=http://www.xeri.com/Moapa/wf-hr-foreword.htm | title=Washingtonia filifera: Nevada's rejected ancient Palm. | publisher=xeri.com | date=1995 | access-date=21 June 2014 | author=Spencer, W.}}</ref><ref name="SpencerPartOne">{{cite web | url=http://www.xeri.com/Moapa/wf-hr-part1.htm | title=A report regarding: The Palm – Washingtonia filifera – in Moapa NV | publisher=xeri.com | date=1995 | access-date=21 June 2014 | author=Spencer, W.}}</ref> The [[apical meristem|bud]] (known as [[heart of palm]]) is also eaten.<ref>{{cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |author-link=Donald C. Peattie |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |year=1953 |publisher=[[Bonanza Books]] |location=New York |page=299}}{{ISBN?}}</ref>

==Access==
[[Joshua Tree National Park]] in the Mojave Desert preserves and protects healthy riparian palm habitat examples in the Little San Bernardino Mountains, and westward where water rises through the San Andreas Fault on the east valley side. One such location is the Fortynine Palms oasis. In the central Coachella Valley, the [[Indio Hills Palms|Indio Hills Palms State Reserve]] and nearby [[Coachella Valley National Wildlife Refuge|Coachella Valley Preserve]], other large oases are protected and accessible. The [[Santa Rosa and San Jacinto Mountains National Monument]], and [[Anza-Borrego Desert State Park]] both have large and diverse ''W. filifera'' canyon oasis habitats.

In Arizona, the largest protected groves of ''Washingtonia filifera'' are found in the lower Bradshaw Mountains at Castle Creek,<ref name=":0" /> where a fenced population is maintained by the Bureau of Land Management. Additional populations occur at the [[Hassayampa River Preserve]], managed by Maricopa County Parks, and at the [https://www.dflt.org/projects-1-2/new-river-nature-reserve New River Preserve], managed by the Desert Foothills Land Trust. A smaller but accessible grove is also protected at [[Kofa National Wildlife Refuge]].

==Cultivation==
''Washingtonia filifera'' is widely cultivated as an [[ornamental tree]]. It is one of the hardiest [[Coryphoideae|coryphoid]] palms, rated as hardy to USDA [[hardiness zone]] 8. It can survive brief temperatures of {{convert|-10|°C|°F}} with minor damage, and established plants have survived, with severe leaf damage, brief periods as low as {{convert|-17|°C|°F}}. The plants grow best in arid or Mediterranean climates, but can be found in humid subtropical climates such as eastern Australia and the southeastern USA. It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/349989/Washingtonia-filifera/Details | title=''Washingtonia filifera'': Washington palm | publisher=Royal Horticultural Society | work=RHS Gardening | access-date=17 March 2021}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web |last=Miller |first=Victor J. |date=1983 |title=Arizona's Own Palm: Washingtonia filifera |url=https://repository.arizona.edu/handle/10150/552211 |website=}}</ref>
